AT&T (NYSE:T) agreed to sell its Mexican wireless operations to Grupo Televisa and Fintech Holdings in a newly announced deal.

The transaction covers AT&T's consumer and enterprise mobile business in Mexico, shifting those subscribers to the two buyers.

Management framed the exit from Mexico as a way to direct more resources toward U.S. fiber and 5G network buildout.

The decision to sell AT&T's Mexican wireless unit is important. Investors also need to weigh other business pressures and capital choices. We have also spotted 4 warning signs (1 major) worth knowing about at AT&T.

NYSE:T Earnings & Revenue Growth as at Oct 2026

AT&T is a large US telecom provider with a market value of about $157.9b. This Mexico exit sits alongside its broader role supplying mobile and technology services across its core domestic network footprint.

4 things going right for AT&T that this headline doesn't cover.

AT&T's Mexico exit puts its fiber‑first bet under a brighter spotlight

AT&T's Narrative is built around a simple trade off. Pour money and management focus into U.S. fiber and 5G, then shrink older networks and lower returning ventures enough that recurring service revenue and cost savings carry the load.

"The key requirement is that AT&T executes on large scale fiber build out, copper retirement, and cost take out while managing device subsidies..."

See how the full story points towards a $29.05 fair value for AT&T.

The Mexico sale leans into the bullish version of that story. Management is choosing to simplify the business model and recycle capital from a non core wireless market into U.S. fiber build, where the Narrative already highlights convergence, copper retirement and recurring service revenue as the main engine. For holders who back that thesis, this looks like alignment rather than a change in direction.

The bear side does not disappear, though. Leaving Mexico trims diversification at a time when analysts already flag high debt, heavy device promotions and earnings that are forecast to decline on current estimates. If Verizon or T Mobile can scale cross border or adjacent services more effectively, AT&T's tighter geographic focus could be read as concentration risk rather than discipline.

In the end, this same transaction can either confirm a cleaner fiber led AT&T story or underline execution and concentration risks, depending on which Narrative you already believe.

So how much of that lost ground could T-Mobile win back over the next three years?

What T-Mobile Shares Would Be Worth On These Assumptions

Under these assumptions, T-Mobile shares would be worth about $226.72 in three years, compared with $157.03 at the October 15, 2026 close. That represents a 44.4% gain before dividends, and it would return the shares to about their highest close of the past year, reached on October 20, 2025.

title: Should You Buy Comcast Stock At Under Seven Times Earnings?
detail:
Should You Buy Comcast Stock At Under Seven Times Earnings?
Trefis Team

Image from Pixabay

Shares of Comcast (CMCSA) currently trade at 6.7 times earnings. That multiple sits at less than a third of the 22.7 times commanded by the median S&P 500 company. Over the past twelve months, the shares fell 19.7%, dividends included. The broader S&P 500 returned 17.3% over that same period. That could signal a sound business on sale, or it might just reflect a fair price for an operation that has stopped growing. So what does a buyer actually get for that price?

Comcast's Spare Cash Is Large Next To Its Price

At that valuation, investors are buying a company that turned 26.0% of its revenue into cash from operations over its latest twelve months. Free cash flow over those same months equaled 23.7% of its market value.

This cash generation relies on a broad set of businesses. Residential Connectivity & Platforms stands as the largest segment, bringing in $70.7 billion of revenue in fiscal 2025. Two smaller divisions posted growth that year. Theme Parks revenue rose 14.1%, and Business Services Connectivity revenue rose 5.5%.

Comcast's Operating Margin Has Fallen To A Ten-Year Low

Comcast is currently keeping less of every sale as profit. The operating margin dropped to 14.7% in the twelve months to June 2026. By contrast, the company averaged a 17.4% margin across the three latest twelve-month periods, this one included. Looking back, Comcast's twelve-month margin has not been lower at any quarter end from fiscal Q3 2016 on.

At the same time, the largest business segment is getting smaller. Revenue in Residential Connectivity & Platforms fell by 0.5% in fiscal 2024, and then fell another 1.2% in fiscal 2025. Media revenue also fell by 3.8% in fiscal 2025. Altogether, total revenue grew only 0.6% in the twelve months to June 2026.

Furthermore, Comcast carries heavy debt. Its total debt equaled 120% of its market value at the latest close. For perspective, total debt across the S&P 500 as a whole stood at just 20.2% of market value.

Is Comcast's Broadband Pivot Lifting Its Margin?

The numbers do not show a lift yet. In fiscal Q2 2026 alone, Comcast recorded an operating margin of 17.2%, compared to 19.8% in fiscal Q2 2025. Revenue fell 1.2% from a year earlier in that quarter. Even so, management noted in its fiscal Q2 2026 results that a strategic pivot in broadband is gaining traction. Management also called that specific period its best wireless quarter ever.

A buyer paying under seven times earnings is not simply betting that the broader market has overlooked a sound business. The buyer is betting that management stops the margin from falling while Comcast keeps producing cash. Investors will get more clarity when the company releases its next report, expected on or around October 22, 2026. This report will detail the operating margin for fiscal Q3 2026. A figure below the 17.7% reported in fiscal Q3 2025 would mean the margin is still falling.

AT&T Inc. (NYSE:T) paid $5.75 billion for the consumer fiber business of Lumen Technologies, Inc. (NASDAQ:LUMN), adding over 1 million subscribers and more than 4 million locations. Buying operating networks accelerates expansion as broadband providers compete to bundle internet and wireless service. For investors exploring the Most Active Blue Chip Stocks to Buy Right Now, AT&T's acquisition highlights how established telecom companies are using strategic deals to expand their networks and strengthen their competitive positions.

At 10x forward earnings, AT&T Inc. (NYSE:T) looks fairly valued if acquired markets deliver cash returns comparable with internally built networks. The purchase price starts the calculation; customer adoption and subsequent spending determine the payoff.

5 Best Telecom Services Stocks to Buy According to Analysts

Ken Wolter / Shutterstock.com

More Customers Must Improve Network Economics

AT&T Inc. (NYSE:T) acquired a footprint with roughly 25% customer penetration, versus 40% across its existing fiber business at year-end 2025. Closing that gap would spread network costs across more paying households. Wireless bundles can improve retention and reduce customer-acquisition spending.

The opportunity for AT&T Inc. (NYSE:T) is turning installed capacity into recurring cash. Cable and fixed-wireless competition can force discounts. Acquired and internally built markets should be compared at similar ages, after installation costs, maintenance and customer churn.

What the Earnings Multiples Capture

September's valuation snapshot puts AT&T Inc. (NYSE:T) at 10x forward P/E versus 8x trailing P/E. Trailing P/E uses past earnings; forward P/E uses forecast earnings. Reported 2025 profits included a $5.6 billion gain from selling the DIRECTV investment, boosting historical earnings. That helps explain why the forward multiple is higher despite expected growth in underlying profits.

A 10x forward P/E places AT&T Inc. (NYSE:T) below its 11x at year-end 2025. Analysts expect normalized EPS of $2.34 in 2026 and $2.57 in 2027, roughly 10% annual growth. Stronger expected earnings support the valuation, while acquisition commitments and declining copper-service revenue warrant restraint. Repurchases also support per-share growth, making operating cash generation an important cross-check.

The Purchase Price Is Only Part of the Bill

AT&T Inc. (NYSE:T) must cover integration, network upgrades, customer connections, and further construction beyond the acquisition payment. These costs determine whether expansion that also increases financing demands improves shareholder returns.
